LONDON, England (CNN) -- A portrait painted 400 years ago and kept anonymously in an Irish home for much of the time since is now believed to be the only painting of William Shakespeare created during his lifetime. The portrait of William Shakespeare is thought to be the "only" portrait painted during his lifetime. "A rather young looking 46, it has to be said," Wells said. Shakespeare died in 1616. The most common portrait of Shakespeare is a gray image showing a bald Bard with a small mustache and beard, and bags under his eyes. The identity of the man in the portrait was lost over the centuries -- until Alec Cobbe saw a portrait from Washington's Folger Shakespeare Library. That painting, which fell into disfavor as a Shakespeare portrait about 70 years ago, turned out to be one of four copies of Cobbe's portrait. The portrait "shows a man wearing expensive costuming, including a very beautifully painted ruff of Italian lacework which would have been very expensive," Wells said. "It establishes, for me, that Shakespeare in his later years was a rather wealthy, a rather well affluent member of aristocratic circles in the society of his time," Wells said. "There's been too much of a tendency to believe that Shakespeare, being the son of a glover, coming for a small town in the middle of England, that he necessarily retained a rather humble status throughout his life." Wells reads even more into what he sees in Shakespeare's newly-found face. "I think it's plausible as a portrait as a good listener, of somebody who would have been capable of writing the plays, clearly the face of a man of high intelligence," he said. "It's the face of a man, I think, who betrays a good deal of wisdom in his features. But, of course, as somebody (King Duncan) says in Shakespeare's story Macbeth, 'there's no art to find the mind's construction in the face.'" It should be noted that Shakespeare's King Duncan paid a price for judging Macbeth to have the face of an honorable man. Macbeth later murdered the king. The public can read Shakespeare's face from the original painting at Shakespeare Birthplace Trust in Stratford-upon-Avon where it goes on display for several months starting April 23. The portrait then returns to the Cobbe family, which inherited it when an ancestor married England's Earl of Southampton -- a friend of Shakespeare who likely commissioned its painting.

Researchers have argued that the portrait was painted around **1610**, when Shakespeare was still alive, and may have served as the model for one of the best-known posthumous images of the writer.

The portrait takes its name from the **Cobbe family**, whose ancestors kept the work for centuries at Newbridge House, near Dublin. Its possible connection to Shakespeare emerged after art experts and literary scholars re-examined the painting’s history, style and relationship to other portraits long associated with the playwright.

If the identification is correct, the discovery would be extraordinary: most accepted images of Shakespeare were created after his death in 1616 or are known through engravings and copies. They pointed to links between the Cobbe family collection and Shakespeare’s patron, **Henry Wriothesley, the 3rd Earl of Southampton**, to whom Shakespeare dedicated his narrative poems “Venus and Adonis” and “The Rape of Lucrece.”

The authentication effort included technical and stylistic analysis, provenance research and comparison with other portraits, including the **Janssen portrait**, another image once believed to show Shakespeare. # Is this the face of Shakespeare? The portrait claim that continues to divide scholars

For more than four centuries, William Shakespeare has been one of the most recognizable names in world literature — and one of its most elusive faces.

Nowhere is that tension clearer than in the debate over the so-called Cobbe portrait, a painting some scholars have claimed is the only surviving portrait of Shakespeare made during his lifetime.

The claim is dramatic: If correct, the image would show Shakespeare not as the familiar balding figure from the First Folio engraving, published seven years after his death, but as a prosperous, fashionable Elizabethan-Jacobean gentleman — with auburn hair, a lace collar and a confident, direct gaze.

But like many discoveries in Shakespeare studies, the story is complicated.

## A portrait hiding in plain sight

The Cobbe portrait takes its name from the Cobbe family, in whose ancestral collection it remained for generations. For many years, the sitter was not identified as Shakespeare. The painting was at times thought to depict another Elizabethan figure, including Sir Walter Raleigh.

That changed in the 2000s, when Alec Cobbe, an art restorer and member of the family, noticed a striking resemblance between the portrait in his family’s collection and another image long associated with Shakespeare: the so-called Janssen portrait, held by the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington, DC.

The Folger painting had been known for centuries as a possible portrait of Shakespeare. It was traditionally attributed to Cornelius Janssen, a prominent portrait painter, though that attribution has been questioned. Over time, alterations to the Folger version — including changes to the hairline — affected how viewers understood the sitter’s appearance.

When the Cobbe portrait was examined alongside the Folger picture and other related versions, supporters of the Shakespeare identification argued that the Cobbe work appeared to be the prime version: the original from which the others were copied.

In 2009, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and leading Shakespeare scholar Stanley Wells publicly backed the claim that the Cobbe portrait showed Shakespeare from life, likely painted around 1610, when the playwright was in his mid-40s.

## Why the Folger copy matters

The Folger copy is central to the debate because it helped bring the Cobbe portrait to scholarly attention.

The Folger Shakespeare Library, home to the world’s largest Shakespeare collection, owns several important Shakespeare-related portraits and artifacts. Its version of the Cobbe-type image had long been part of the broader conversation about Shakespeare’s likeness, even if its authenticity was uncertain.

The resemblance between the Folger painting and the Cobbe portrait suggested that both belonged to a group of related images. Advocates of the Cobbe claim say the Folger version is a later copy of the Cobbe original — evidence, they argue, that the image was once considered significant enough to replicate.

But the existence of copies does not settle the identity of the sitter. Portraits of noblemen, courtiers and patrons were frequently copied in the period, and likenesses could be reidentified over time. For skeptics, the Folger connection proves only that the Cobbe portrait had a visual afterlife — not that it depicts Shakespeare.

## The Earl of Southampton connection

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the Cobbe portrait’s backstory is its possible link to Henry Wriothesley, the 3rd Earl of Southampton.

Southampton is one of the most important figures in Shakespeare’s early career. Shakespeare dedicated two narrative poems to him: “Venus and Adonis” in 1593 and “The Rape of Lucrece” in 1594. The dedications are unusually warm, and Southampton has often been described as Shakespeare’s patron.

Supporters of the Cobbe identification argue that the portrait may have descended through the Southampton family before entering the Cobbe collection. If true, that provenance would be significant. A portrait of Shakespeare in the possession of Southampton or his descendants would make historical sense, given the known literary connection between the playwright and the aristocrat.

The Cobbe family’s collection included works with links to Southampton’s descendants, and proponents say this strengthens the case that the portrait could have originated in circles close to Shakespeare.

Still, provenance from the early 17th century is difficult to prove conclusively. The chain of ownership is suggestive, not airtight.

## A face unlike the familiar Shakespeare

One reason the Cobbe portrait attracted so much attention is that it presents a different Shakespeare from the one many people know.

The most authoritative early likeness of Shakespeare is generally considered to be the engraving by Martin Droeshout in the 1623 First Folio, the first collected edition of Shakespeare’s plays. Although the engraving was published after Shakespeare’s death, it was approved by people who knew him, including his fellow actors and editors John Heminges and Henry Condell.

Another important image is the funerary monument bust in Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon, where Shakespeare is buried. Like the Droeshout engraving, it dates from the years shortly after his death and has long shaped the public image of the playwright.

The Cobbe portrait, by contrast, shows a more refined and courtly figure. That has appealed to some scholars, who see it as consistent with Shakespeare’s success by around 1610: a wealthy playwright, shareholder in the King’s Men and property owner in Stratford.

Others argue the sitter looks more like a courtier than a writer — though in Shakespeare’s world, those categories were not always as visually distinct as modern viewers might imagine.

## The case for — and against

The argument for the Cobbe portrait rests on several points: its apparent date, its relationship to the Folger and other copies, its possible Southampton provenance, and its resemblance — debated though it is — to accepted Shakespeare likenesses.

Supporters say the painting’s age and network of copies suggest it was an important portrait from Shakespeare’s lifetime. They also point to the Southampton connection as a plausible explanation for why such an image might have been commissioned or preserved.

Critics are unconvinced. They note that no inscription on the Cobbe portrait definitively identifies the sitter as Shakespeare. They also caution that resemblance is subjective, especially when comparing portraits from different artists and media.

In the world of Tudor and Jacobean portraiture, mistaken identities are common. Many portraits were relabeled generations after they were painted, sometimes based on family tradition rather than documentary proof.

For skeptics, the Cobbe portrait remains an interesting candidate — but not a settled discovery.

## A Shakespeare mystery that endures

The debate over the Cobbe portrait reflects a larger fascination with Shakespeare himself. Despite the survival of his plays, poems, legal records and business documents, the man behind the works remains tantalizingly distant.

That distance has made portraits especially powerful. A confirmed lifetime image of Shakespeare would offer something rare: a direct visual encounter with the playwright as his contemporaries may have seen him.

For now, the Cobbe portrait occupies a disputed but prominent place in that search. To its supporters, it is the only surviving painting of Shakespeare made from life. To its critics, it is a compelling but unproven likeness of an unidentified Jacobean gentleman.

Either way, the painting has done what few portraits can: it has reopened the question of what William Shakespeare looked like — and reminded the world how much about him is still unresolved.
